claims.source: For example, the most common RCC histology, clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC), is characterized by biallelic loss of the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) tumor suppressor and subsequent activation of hypoxia inducible factor (HIF), suppressing mitochondrial respiration in favor of glycolytic metabolism.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about ccRCC molecular characteristics.

claims.claim: Chromophobe RCCs and renal oncocytomas are characterized by loss-of-function mutations in the mitochondrial genome resulting in accumulation of respiration-defective mitochondria (Joshi et al., 2015).
claims.source: Similarly, chRCCs and renal oncocytomas are characterized by loss-of-function mutations in the mitochondrial genome resulting in accumulation of respiration-defective mitochondria (Joshi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on chRCC and oncocytoma molecular characteristics.

claims.claim: Inactivating mutations to genes essential for mtDNA replication, maintenance, and biosynthesis (e.g. POLG, TK2) can result in severe depletion of mtDNA and cause autosomally recessive heritable disorders (El-Hattab and Scaglia, 2013).
claims.source: It is known that inactivating mutations to genes which are essential for mtDNA replication, maintenance, and biosynthesis (e.g. POLG, TK2) can result in severe depletion of mtDNA and cause autosomally recessive heritable disorders (El-Hattab and Scaglia, 2013).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on mtDNA depletion disorders.

claims.claim: Sorbitol accumulation has been observed in the blood of patients with progressive external ophthalmoplegia (Esterhuizen et al., 2017).
claims.source: Furthermore, studies of metabolomic changes associated with mitochondrial disease indicate that sorbitol accumulation is not a generic consequence of mitochondrial dysfunction, although its elevation has been observed in the blood of patients with progressive external ophthalmoplegia (Esterhuizen et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on metabolomic changes in mitochondrial disease.

claims.claim: Lactate levels in CCPAP tumors were not elevated relative to normal tissue or ccRCC.
claims.source: Specifically, lactate levels in CCPAP tumors were not elevated relative to normal tissue or ccRCC, nor were any other intermediates of glycolysis (Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements of lactate and glycolytic intermediates.

claims.claim: ccRCC and papillary RCC (pRCC) are believed to derive from proximal tubule cells based on gene expression data.
claims.source: On the basis of gene expression data, ccRCC and papillary RCC (pRCC) are believed to derive from proximal tubule cells, while chromophobe RCC (chRCC) is believed to arise from the distal tubule.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression data about cell-of-origin.

claims.claim: Chromophobe RCC (chRCC) is believed to arise from the distal tubule based on gene expression data.
claims.source: On the basis of gene expression data, ccRCC and papillary RCC (pRCC) are believed to derive from proximal tubule cells, while chromophobe RCC (chRCC) is believed to arise from the distal tubule.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on inference from gene expression data about cell-of-origin.

claims.claim: CCPAP tumors resemble cells of the collecting duct based on comparison of transcriptomic profiles with microdissected regions of mouse kidney (Cheval et al., 2012).
claims.source: Doing so, we found that while ccRCC and pRCC tumors most resemble cells of the proximal tubule and chRCC tumors resemble cells of the distal tubule, CCPAP tumors resemble cells of the collecting duct (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on comparison of transcriptomic profiles with mouse kidney data.

claims.claim: CCPAP tumors stain positive for the collecting duct marker 34BE12 (Cheval et al., 2012).
claims.source: This is consistent with prior immunohistochemical findings showing that CCPAP tumors stain positive for the collecting duct marker 34BE12 (Cheval et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior immunohistochemical findings.

claims.claim: CCPAP tumors display upregulated HIF1 protein as well as elevated levels of downstream HIF targets (CA9, GLUT1) by IHC staining despite wild-type VHL and TCEB1 (Rohan et al., 2011).
claims.source: An interesting aspect of CCPAP RCC is that despite wild-type VHL and TCEB1, CCPAP tumors display upregulated HIF1 protein as well as elevated levels of downstream HIF targets (CA9, GLUT1) by IHC staining (Rohan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior immunohistochemical findings.

claims.claim: High levels of oxidative stress could inhibit prolyl hydroxylase (PHD) activity to prevent the hydroxylation of HIF and subsequent VHL-dependent degradation (Mansfield et al., 2005; Pan et al., 2007).
claims.source: Conceivably, high levels of oxidative stress could inhibit prolyl hydroxylase (PHD) activity to prevent the hydroxylation of HIF and subsequent VHL-dependent degradation (Mansfield et al., 2005; Pan et al., 2007), which would be responsible for HIF activation in CCPAP.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative and based on citation of prior literature on PHD inhibition by oxidative stress.

claims.claim: Both HIF activation and oxidative stress have been shown to cause mtDNA depletion (Zhang et al., 2007; Mansouri et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2001; Suliman et al., 2003; Shokolenko et al., 2009).
claims.source: Interestingly, both HIF activation and oxidative stress have been shown to cause mtDNA depletion (Zhang et al., 2007; Mansouri et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2001; Suliman et al., 2003; Shokolenko et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on causes of mtDNA depletion.

claims.claim: CCPAP tumors exhibit severe depletion of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and RNA.
claims.source: In spite of a largely wild-type nuclear genome, CCPAP tumors exhibit severe depletion of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and RNA and high levels of oxidative stress, reflecting a shift away from respiratory metabolism.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including mtDNA copy number analysis and mtRNA expression analysis.

claims.claim: CCPAP tumors exhibit high levels of oxidative stress.
claims.source: In spite of a largely wild-type nuclear genome, CCPAP tumors exhibit severe depletion of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and RNA and high levels of oxidative stress, reflecting a shift away from respiratory metabolism.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements (elevated glutathione, ophthalmate) and immunohistochemical staining (8-oxo-dG).

claims.claim: CCPAP tumors exhibit a distinct metabolic phenotype uniquely characterized by accumulation of the sugar alcohol sorbitol.
claims.source: Moreover, CCPAP tumors exhibit a distinct metabolic phenotype uniquely characterized by accumulation of the sugar alcohol sorbitol.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic measurements showing high sorbitol levels in CCPAP.

claims.claim: CCPAP tumors reflect a shift away from respiratory metabolism.
claims.source: In spite of a largely wild-type nuclear genome, CCPAP tumors exhibit severe depletion of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and RNA and high levels of oxidative stress, reflecting a shift away from respiratory metabolism.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combination of mtDNA/mtRNA depletion, downregulation of oxidative phosphorylation genes, and reduced levels of mitochondrial metabolites.

claims.claim: Elevation of glutathione is generically observed across many RCC histologies, including but not limited to clear-cell, chromophobe, and oncocytomas (Hakimi et al., 2016; Gopal et al., 2018; Priolo et al., 2018).
claims.source: Importantly, data from our group and others have repeatedly demonstrated that elevation of glutathione is generically observed across many RCC histologies, including but not limited to clear-cell, chromophobe, and oncocytomas (Hakimi et al., 2016; Gopal et al., 2018; Priolo et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on citation of prior literature on glutathione levels in RCC.

claims.claim: An elevated response to oxidative stress is particularly pronounced in CCPAP tumors.
claims.source: Our data here suggests that an elevated response to oxidative stress is particularly pronounced in CCPAP tumors, but cannot be used to distinguish them from other histologies.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomic and immunohistochemical data showing high levels of oxidative stress markers in CCPAP.

results.result: CCPAP tumors were identified as metabolic outliers in a ccRCC dataset through t-SNE analysis, confirmed by pathological review, and distinguished by approximately 30-fold accumulation of sorbitol. Validation in an independent cohort showed CCPAP samples form a distinct metabolic cluster from ccRCC, with clustering driven by metabolic features beyond sorbitol alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide converging evidence from discovery (C1-C3) and validation (C4-C5) cohorts. The t-SNE analysis is supported by visual data (Figures 1A-B), pathological confirmation (C2), and metabolomic measurements (C3). The control experiment with high-sorbitol ccRCC samples (C5) strengthens the conclusion that CCPAP's distinct clustering reflects broader metabolic differences beyond sorbitol alone.

results.result: CCPAP exhibits a distinct metabolic profile with 200 differentially abundant metabolites compared to ccRCC (152 vs. normal tissue), characterized by elevated sorbitol (8.5-fold vs. ccRCC, 36-fold vs. normal), other sugar alcohols (4-fold), glutathione (>12-fold), and ophthalmate (4-fold), alongside broad downregulation of glycerophosphoethanolamines.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C13 are supported by comprehensive metabolomic profiling with appropriate statistical testing (Mann-Whitney with FDR correction, q<0.1). The measurements are quantitative, internally consistent, and show clear patterns of metabolic reprogramming. Multiple independent metabolite classes support the conclusion of distinct CCPAP metabolism.

results.result: CCPAP tumors show distinct glycolytic and polyol pathway metabolism compared to ccRCC: normal levels of upper glycolysis metabolites (G6P, F6P) but >30-fold elevation of polyol pathway metabolites (sorbitol, fructose) and elevated NADH/NAD ratio, suggesting preferential carbon flux through the polyol pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 are supported by metabolomic measurements mapped onto metabolic pathways (Figure 2B). The pattern of normal upper glycolysis with elevated polyol pathway metabolites and NADH/NAD ratio is internally consistent and supported by additional analysis of NAD-dependent reactions (Figure 2—supplement 2). However, the authors appropriately note that metabolite abundance does not directly measure flux.

results.result: CCPAP tumors exhibit severe mitochondrial dysfunction characterized by mtDNA depletion (among lowest 4 samples in TCGA), >2-fold reduction in mtRNA vs. ccRCC, >3-fold reduction vs. normal tissue, downregulation of 411 nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes, and downregulation of oxidative phosphorylation gene sets with upregulation of hypoxic response genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C25 provide multiple converging lines of evidence for mitochondrial dysfunction from TCGA data: mtDNA copy number (C22), mtRNA expression (C23-C24), nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene expression (C25), and pathway analysis (C20-C21). The statistical tests are appropriate (Mann-Whitney p=0.016, t-test p=0.0002 and p=10^-6), and the findings are internally consistent across different analytical approaches.

results.result: CCPAP tumors show reduced levels of mitochondria-dependent metabolites: 3.5-fold reduction in aspartate and 4-fold reduction in fumarate relative to normal tissue, consistent with impaired mitochondrial respiratory chain function.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by metabolomic measurements (Figure 3D) and are consistent with the broader pattern of mitochondrial dysfunction established by other claims. The metabolites selected (aspartate, fumarate) are appropriate markers of mitochondrial function, and the reductions are substantial and statistically significant.

results.result: CCPAP tumors have a remarkably quiet nuclear genome characterized by low mutational burden compared to ccRCC, wild-type VHL and TCEB1 in all samples, no recurrently mutated genes, and minimal copy number alterations (no arm-level changes).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 are supported by comprehensive genomic analysis including WGS (n=5) and WES (n=5 including TCGA). The findings are visualized in Figure 4A-C and show consistent patterns across samples. The FACETS algorithm for copy number analysis is appropriate and well-cited. The absence of recurrent alterations is a negative finding but is well-supported by the data.

results.result: CCPAP tumors show ~10-fold mtDNA depletion relative to normal kidney without evidence of causative genetic alterations: no mutations in mtDNA maintenance genes, no differential expression of maintenance genes, and <1 non-synonymous mtDNA mutation per tumor (all missense, non-deleterious) by ultra-deep sequencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 systematically rule out common genetic causes of mtDNA depletion through multiple approaches: nuclear gene mutations (C33), gene expression changes (C34), and mtDNA mutations (C35-C36). The ultra-deep duplex sequencing (C35) is a rigorous method for detecting low-frequency variants. The ~10-fold depletion (C32) is well-quantified from sequencing data. The negative findings are appropriately interpreted as suggesting cryptic or non-genetic mechanisms.

results.result: CCPAP tumors co-localize with adjacent-normal kidney tissue rather than ccRCC tumors in principal components analysis of DNA methylation data, suggesting CCPAP resembles normal kidney from a methylation perspective.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 is supported by PCA analysis of TCGA 450K methylation data (Figure 5—supplement 1B) from 4 CCPAP samples. The analysis is appropriate and the finding is clearly visualized. However, the sample size is small (n=4) and the interpretation is limited to methylation patterns at CpG islands.

results.result: CCPAP tumors show significantly reduced protein expression of both mtDNA-encoded (MT-CO1) and nuclear-encoded mitochondrial (TOM20) proteins by immunohistochemistry, with CCPAP having the lowest MT-CO1 H-score among RCC subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by quantitative IHC analysis (Figure 5A-B) with appropriate statistical testing (t-test, p<0.01 to p<0.0001). The findings validate the transcriptomic and metabolomic evidence of mitochondrial dysfunction at the protein level. The tissue microarray analysis (C39) provides broader context across RCC subtypes (n=11 CCPAP, n=7 ccRCC, n=2 pRCC, n=4 chRCC, n=4 oncocytoma).

results.result: CCPAP tumors exhibit elevated oxidative stress markers including upregulated miR200 family, highest 8-oxo-dG H-score among RCC subtypes by IHC, but without enrichment of C:G>A:T mutations, suggesting oxidative stress is being managed by cellular stress responses without causing excess oxidative DNA damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 provide converging evidence for oxidative stress (C40-C42) with an important caveat about mutation signatures (C43). The miRNA analysis (C40) is consistent with prior literature, IHC quantification (C41-C42) shows significant differences (p<0.05), and mutation signature analysis (C43) appropriately distinguishes oxidative stress from oxidative DNA damage. The interpretation that stress responses prevent mutagenesis is reasonable but somewhat speculative.

results.result: CCPAP and ccRCC both contain cytoplasmic glycogen (PAS/PAS-diastase positive), but CCPAP tumors are Oil Red O negative and depleted of lipid classes by metabolomics, indicating cytoplasmic clarity in CCPAP arises from glycogen rather than lipid accumulation as in ccRCC.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C48 integrate histochemical staining (C44-C45, Figure 5E) with metabolomic data (C46-C47) to explain the morphological feature of cytoplasmic clarity. The evidence is internally consistent: both tumor types have glycogen, but only ccRCC has lipids. The conclusion (C48) is well-supported by the combination of techniques, though it is somewhat inferential.

results.result: CCPAP tumors do not show elevated lactate or other glycolytic intermediates relative to normal tissue or ccRCC, indicating absence of compensatory upregulation of glycolysis despite mitochondrial dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claim C66 is supported by metabolomic measurements (Figure 2, source data 1). This negative finding is important as it distinguishes CCPAP from classical Warburg metabolism and is consistent with the indolent nature of these tumors. The measurement is straightforward and the interpretation is appropriate.

results.result: CCPAP tumors resemble collecting duct cells based on transcriptomic comparison with microdissected mouse kidney regions, consistent with positive staining for collecting duct marker 34BE12.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by transcriptomic correlation analysis (Figure 5—supplement 3) and prior IHC literature (C70). The approach of comparing tumor profiles to normal kidney cell types is reasonable for inferring cell-of-origin. However, the cross-species comparison (human tumors to mouse kidney) introduces some uncertainty, and the IHC evidence (C70) is from prior literature rather than this study.

results.result: CCPAP tumors exhibit a comprehensive molecular phenotype characterized by severe mtDNA/mtRNA depletion, high oxidative stress, distinct sorbitol accumulation, and shift away from respiratory metabolism, despite a largely wild-type nuclear genome.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C78 represent summary statements integrating multiple lines of evidence from other claim groups. Each component is well-supported by the detailed claims: mtDNA/RNA depletion (C22-C25, C32), oxidative stress (C11-C12, C40-C42), sorbitol accumulation (C3, C8-C9, C77), and respiratory dysfunction (C20-C27). The integration is appropriate and represents the major conclusions of the study.

results.result: Prior literature establishes CCPAP as a rare, indolent RCC subtype initially described in ESRD but also occurring in normal kidney function, characterized by distinctive morphology (linear nuclear orientation, low-grade features), absence of VHL/3p deletion and pRCC-associated chromosomal changes, with no identified genetic drivers.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C56 summarize prior literature on CCPAP clinical and molecular features. All claims are appropriately cited to peer-reviewed publications (Tickoo 2006, Rohan 2011, Gobbo 2008, Williamson 2013, Ross 2012, Adam 2011, Lawrie 2014). This background information provides essential context for the current study's findings. The citations appear appropriate and the characterization is consistent with the referenced literature.

results.result: Nearly 8% of tumors in the institution's prospective sequencing cohort show no alterations in 341 cancer-associated genes, illustrating the prevalence of cancers without identifiable genetic drivers.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by data from the institution's MSK-IMPACT clinical sequencing cohort (Zehir et al., 2017). This provides important context for why non-genomic profiling approaches are valuable. The statistic is clearly stated and appropriately cited.

results.result: Prior literature establishes that metabolic enzyme mutations (FH, SDH, IDH) and mitochondrial dysfunction are recurrent themes in cancer biology, with specific relevance to RCC subtypes (ccRCC with VHL/HIF, chRCC/oncocytomas with mtDNA mutations), and that mtDNA depletion can result from nuclear gene mutations in hereditary disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 provide literature context on metabolic reprogramming in cancer and RCC. All claims are appropriately cited to peer-reviewed publications (Wallace 2012, Warburg 1956, Vyas 2016, Zong 2016, Grandhi 2017, Joshi 2015, El-Hattab 2013, Esterhuizen 2017). This background establishes the conceptual framework for interpreting CCPAP's metabolic phenotype within the broader context of cancer metabolism and RCC biology.

results.result: Prior literature shows CCPAP displays HIF activation despite wild-type VHL/TCEB1, with speculation that oxidative stress could inhibit PHD activity to stabilize HIF, and that both HIF activation and oxidative stress can cause mtDNA depletion.
results.evaluation: Claim C71 is supported by prior literature (Rohan 2011), but C72 is explicitly speculative ("Conceivably...") and based on cited mechanisms (Mansfield 2005, Pan 2007) rather than direct evidence in CCPAP. Claim C73 cites literature on causes of mtDNA depletion but doesn't demonstrate these mechanisms operate in CCPAP. The causal relationships proposed are plausible but not directly tested in this study.

results.result: Elevated glutathione is observed across many RCC histologies, but the oxidative stress response is particularly pronounced in CCPAP tumors, though this cannot distinguish CCPAP from other RCC subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C80 appropriately contextualize the glutathione findings. C79 is well-cited to prior literature (Hakimi 2016, Gopal 2018, Priolo 2018), and C80 is supported by the metabolomic and IHC data in this study (C11-C12, C41-C42). The authors appropriately note the limitation that oxidative stress markers alone cannot distinguish CCPAP from other RCC types.
